content: Discharge refers to an exudate that drains from wounds, which can be either internal or external in origin. It is formed from serum. Serous Discharge Serous discharge is clear or straw-colored in appearance. It originates from protein and fluid present in the tissue. This type of discharge supports the healing process and contains protein, electrolytes, sugar, and white blood cells. It is a normal part of the wound healing process. Sanguinous Discharge Sanguinous discharge is red in color and results from trauma to a blood vessel. It may occur during wound cleaning or when a wound is disturbed. The consistency of this discharge is thin and watery, containing sanguinous fluid. The red appearance is due to the presence of red blood cells in the discharge. Serosanguinous Discharge Serosanguinous discharge appears pink because a small number of blood cells mix with serous drainage. It has a thin, water-like consistency. This type of discharge is a normal occurrence during the healing of wounds. Purulent Discharge Purulent discharge is yellow, gray, or green in color. It is produced when an infection is present. The fluid contains infectious microbes, white blood cells, and other inflammatory cells. The volume of this exudate increases with prolonged infection. Mucopurulent Discharge Mucopurulent discharge consists of pus mixed with mucoid cells. It appears as a whitish-yellow or yellow substance produced during the body’s inflammatory response. It is commonly observed in areas affected by pyogenic bacterial infections. This discharge contains a thin, protein-rich fluid known as liquor puris, along with dead neutrophils (white blood cells), which are part of the body’s innate immune response. Hemorrhagic Discharge Hemorrhagic discharge indicates active bleeding from a leaking blood vessel. Its consistency is thicker than that of sanguinous fluid. In some cases, surgical intervention may be required to control the bleeding.
